[0] everyday_reading (E): Everyday meaning: 'run the program' as if the file ran itself, or the program 'looks at all of itself at once'. Java rule: java Name starts the JVM, which calls Name's main() and executes its statements one at a time, in order.
[1] misconception (M) -> CompileRunsProgram: wrong rule: Compiling also executes the program. Right rule: The program runs only when java Name is typed; javac only translates it.
[2] inconsistent_trace (T) -> CompileRunsProgram: Applies the run rule (LT: main's statements execute in order, one by one, each once) unevenly: e.g. executes the print statements in written order on one trace but skips one or reorders them on another. (here mixing in: "compiling also executes the program")

[0] names_the_element (N): Running (executing) a program is launching it with java Name so that the Java Virtual Machine follows its instructions.
[1] states_the_rule (S): Typing java followed by a class name makes the system call the main() method defined in that class and execute its statements; java Name args... also passes the command-line arguments to main. The development cycle is the same in any environment (terminal or IDE): edit the .java file, compile it with javac, run it with java.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): The JVM starts at the first statement of main and ends when it finishes the last statement; statements run one by one, in order, and control returns to the system when main finishes.
[1] output_prediction (OP): The result of a run is what the program prints to the terminal (for java HelloWorld: Hello, World), or an exception message if a run-time error occurs.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): One execution step runs one statement of main, which changes the program state (a variable or the output) and passes control to the next statement.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): java Name runs the Name.class that javac produced, so compiling must succeed first; the run reflects the source as of the last successful compile.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): A run-time error appears only while java Name executes; the JVM stops the program and prints the exception.
[2] relation_to_neighbour (R): A logic error is seen only by running the program and comparing its output with the intended output.
[3] relation_to_neighbour (R): A program is tested by running it on chosen inputs and comparing what it prints with what it should print.
[4] relation_to_neighbour (R): Each small step is run and checked before the next one is added.
[5] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Purpose: make the computer carry out the program on particular inputs; running the same compiled program with different command-line arguments gives different results.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> CompileRunsProgram: Running again with the same arguments reproduces the same output (for programs without randomness or input); changing the arguments changes the output without recompiling; editing the source changes nothing until recompiled.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Run the program to test it on chosen inputs and to see run-time and logic errors that compiling cannot find; adding print statements and rerunning is a simple way to check what is actually executing.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: In the book's setup a StdAudio program should end main() with System.exit(0). Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: a program that uses StdAudio and finishes main without System.exit(0): the terminal hangs and needs <ctrl-c>
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Run only after a successful compile; java takes a class name. Kind: launch error. Trigger class: running java Name when Name.class is missing or stale, or typing java Name.java
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A required command-line argument must be typed. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: running a program that reads args[0] with no argument

wrong: If javac Name.java finishes without errors, the program already works and has run. | right: javac only translates Name.java into Name.class; the program runs only with java Name, and run-time errors can still appear then.
